claims.claim: The ownership form of a business is its legal structure, which determines who owns the business, who is liable for its debts, and how its profits are taxed.
The four forms most commonly discussed are sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, and limited liability company (LLC).
A sole proprietorship is a business established, owned, operated, and often financed by one person, who keeps all the profits and is personally liable for all the debts.
A partnership is an association of two or more individuals who agree to operate a business together for profit and share its profits and losses; it is relatively simple to set up.
A corporation is a legal entity separate from its owners that can own property, enter contracts, and be sued in its own name, and its owners are not personally liable for its debts.

A limited liability company (LLC) is a hybrid organization that combines features of partnerships and corporations; it appeals to small businesses because it is easy to set up while offering the liability protection of a corporation.
The main trade-offs between ownership forms are liability, taxes, control, and paperwork.
There is no single best ownership form; owners should first consider their needs and goals and understand the features of each form before choosing.
A business can convert to a different business structure in the future, but the change may be subject to restrictions and can bring tax consequences and other complications.
Founders make the ownership decision, and consulting business counselors, attorneys, and accountants is standard helpful practice (general guidance, not legal advice).

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many 'main' forms exist: OpenStax presents sole proprietorship, partnership, and corporation as the three main forms with LLCs among specialized options, while CFI lists four main forms including the LLC and SBA adds further variants (S corporations, LPs, LLPs).
positions: OpenStax: three main forms plus specialized forms including LLC
CFI: four main forms including LLC
SBA: several structures including C corp, S corp, partnership types, LLC
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the four forms most commonly discussed (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, LLC) and notes that other arrangements exist; each named form has its own sibling topic that owns the depth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Tax treatment descriptions (e.g., corporate double taxation) are jurisdiction-specific in the sources (U.S. context).
positions: OpenStax and SBA describe double taxation of corporate profits and dividends as a U.S. phenomenon
Other jurisdictions structure entity taxation differently
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson keeps tax treatment at the level of a general trade-off (profits taxed at the business level vs. flowing to owners) and states no jurisdiction-specific rule as universal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Terminology: 'unlimited liability' (OpenStax) versus 'personal liability' (SBA) for owner exposure.
positions: OpenStax: sole proprietors face unlimited liability
SBA: sole proprietors can be held personally liable
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'personally liable / personal liability' as the general concept and explains it with examples (owner's own assets exposed), avoiding jurisdiction-loaded phrasing.

sourceRecords.title: Choose a business structure
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (page served at the canonical URL; redirect followed to the counseling launch guide which contains the business-structure section). Supports: the business structure affects taxes, ability to raise money, paperwork, and personal liability; sole proprietorship as the automatic default when doing business without registering another form; partnerships as the simplest structure for two or more owners; the corporation as a legal entity separate from its owners offering the strongest liability protection at higher formation cost and more record-keeping; the LLC as combining corporation and partnership benefits with personal-asset protection in most instances; conversion to a different structure is possible but may carry restrictions, tax consequences, and other complications; consulting business counselors, attorneys, and accountants can prove helpful. Facts synthesized into original prose; no wording reproduced. U.S. context framed as such.
